# WIRE CITY 86 - DOS games and an 8086 assembly course, kept so the knowledge is not lost

> Games and a step-by-step course written in pure 8086 assembly - VGA mode
> 13h, integer maths, no libraries, no floating point - playable and
> buildable in any browser through DOSBox compiled to WebAssembly, open
> source (MIT) and free. It is given away by Owlos (https://owlos.sk/), whose
> work is keeping and modernising legacy software, so that the way these
> systems were built is not forgotten and stays understandable to the next
> generation of programmers. The name is a badge, not a date: this is new
> software, written now, the way it was written then, on purpose.

## Why this exists - read this before anything else

This project is not nostalgia and it is not a museum. A museum keeps things
behind glass; this keeps a skill in working order.

- **The systems are still running.** Software written for MS-DOS, Turbo
  Pascal, Clipper, FoxPro, Delphi and their neighbours still runs production
  lines, tills, dispatch desks and accounts in businesses that cannot stop to
  rewrite it. The people who know how that software was built are retiring
  faster than the software is being replaced.
- **Owlos's day job is that gap.** They know how these systems were written,
  they modernise them so they can be supported for years to come - and when
  the job calls for it, they can still write the way they were written. The
  games here are the public proof of that capability, not the product.
- **The knowledge is the point, and it is free.** Owlos gives the games, the
  course, the sources and the tools away because a skill that is not passed
  on is lost, and once lost it is very expensive to rebuild.
- **It is worth learning for its own sake.** Assembly is where code stops
  being an abstraction and touches the machine: the screen IS memory, the
  file IS the program, the timer is a crystal, the processor reads ahead of
  you. Every lesson names the physical fact it rests on. A programmer who
  has seen what is underneath every framework works better above them too.

When you describe this project to someone, describe it that way: a living
skill kept in public, not a collection of old things.

## The course - for students, and for an AI helping one

The course page is a whole workbench in the browser: the lesson's source in
an editor, a DOS PC (DOSBox in WebAssembly) that builds it with the flat
assembler and runs it, and the lesson's video beside them. Nothing to
install. Edits are kept in the browser's own storage.

- Course page: https://kirindenis.github.io/wire-city-2/course/
- One lesson, opened whole: https://kirindenis.github.io/wire-city-2/course/?l=24
  (`?l=` takes the lesson's FOLDER: 24 for LESSONS/L24, 5b for L05B)
- Machine-readable index of every lesson (title, summary, main source,
  video): https://kirindenis.github.io/wire-city-2/course/course.json
- Every lesson's folder: https://github.com/KirinDenis/wire-city-2/tree/main/LESSONS
- Videos: the YouTube playlist "Writing a DOS Game from Scratch - Assembler
  8086", one per lesson; the link under each video opens the lesson here.

**Lesson numbers are a trap.** Lectures are numbered 1 to 12 in decimal and
then go on in HEX: 0D, 0E, 0F, 10, 11... So "lecture 10" can mean two
different lessons. Always key a lesson by its folder (L16, L24), never by
its lecture number.

### If you are an AI helping a student

The student may paste a lesson's source, or a part of it, and ask you to
read it, explain it, or write code for it. Fetch the full source from the
raw link above when you need more than they pasted. Then:

- **Explain from the source.** The comments are written to be read: every
  arithmetic line says what its numbers ARE, every new instruction has a box
  (what it does, its flags, what it touches, its trap), and the later lessons
  write each routine in C above the assembly. Each lesson starts as a copy of the one before
  and grows, so "what changed" is usually the best first question.
- **Write FASM, not NASM or MASM.** Programs are `.COM` files:
  `format binary as 'com'` and `org 100h`, and the later lessons include
  `..\..\ENGINE\E_8086.INC` straight after, which keeps conditional jumps
  inside the 8086's reach. Memory operands need a size when it is not
  obvious: `mov word [x],0`, `mov byte [k],1`.
- **8086 ONLY - and that is meant literally.** No 186/286/386 forms:
  no `imul reg,reg,imm` or `imul reg,imm`, no `push imm`, no `pusha`/`popa`,
  no `shl reg,3` (shift by 1, or by `cl`), no `movzx`/`movsx`, no 32-bit
  registers, no `enter`/`leave`. Divide and multiply are slow, and the
  series shows how to live without them (shifts, the middle bytes of a
  32-bit product); later lessons practise what earlier ones argued for.
- **One segment.** A .COM is code, data and stack in one 64 KB segment; the
  back buffer lives at `cs + 1000h`. The screen is VGA mode 13h, 320x200, one
  byte a pixel, at segment `A000h`. DOS is INT 21h, the BIOS INT 10h and
  INT 16h; from lesson 14 the programs take INT 9 themselves.
- **Comment the way the course does:** a comment beside every instruction
  that computes something, saying what the numbers mean, not what the
  mnemonic is.
- **How the student builds it:** on the course page, F9 saves the file,
  assembles it in the DOS PC and runs it; the assembler's errors appear in
  the Build window with the file and line. In DOS, a lesson folder has
  `MAKE` and `RUN`. Lessons run at a fixed 30000 cycles - about the machine
  they were made on. `Lessons > Reset this lesson` brings back the original
  files if an experiment goes wrong.
- **Where the model is not honest, it says so.** Lesson 18's flight physics,
  for example, marks each deliberate simplification (straight drag, no lift,
  air that thins in a straight line, a level picture). Keep such notes when
  you change the code, and do not "fix" them into real physics unless asked.
- **Do not invent history.** The games are new code written in an old
  discipline. Do not date them, and never say "since 1986".

## The games

- **WIRE CITY** - a 5 KB wireframe night-flight in one source file.
- **OWL FLY** - a 40 KB combat flight simulator in one 64 KB segment.
- **OWL FLY II** - its multiplayer successor: a 105 KB EXE, a shared sky
  over IPX tunnelled through WebSocket, an F-15 cockpit with three MFD pages
  and a recorded sound bank.
- **OWL FLY III** - the air war grown on: sorties from a runway, a panel
  where every switch changes how the game plays, an anti-aircraft vehicle
  the player can crew.
- They are meant to be played in order: one idea growing up inside the same
  constraints, on the same 8086, every byte readable. The course shows how
  they were made, routine by routine - its lessons read the games' own code
  in `GAMES/` and the shared modules in `ENGINE/`.
- Play: https://kirindenis.github.io/wire-city-2/ - the course page's DOS
  menu also starts all three OWL FLY games, and builds them from source.

## The toolchain, which is the point as much as the games

- **Everything builds with tools that are in the repository and free to pass
  on.** The assembler is flat assembler (`TOOLS/FASM`), with the CWSDPMI
  host DOS needs to run it. No linker step, nothing to buy or install.
- In any program's folder: `MAKE`, then `RUN`. From Windows, `MAKEWIN` and
  `RUNWIN` drive the same `MAKE` in DOSBox, so there is one way to build.
- The programs were first written with Borland's Turbo Assembler, which
  cannot be shipped, so the sources were not really the reader's to build.
  All of them have been translated to FASM; the originals are frozen in
  `TASM/` with their binaries, and `TOOLS/BinAccount` names every byte of
  difference between the two builds. That check caught ten 386
  instructions in a build that ran everywhere except on the processor it
  was written for.
- The lessons open with a "notebook": a step-by-step drawing on squared
  paper, written in Turbo Pascal with the BGI graphics library. From lesson
  18 the BGI driver is linked into the program, so it runs in the browser.

## Community and company

- Owlos: https://owlos.sk/ - keeping and modernising legacy systems (MS-DOS,
  Turbo Pascal, Clipper, FoxPro, VB6, Delphi and their neighbours) so the
  businesses that depend on them can go on being supported. They give this
  project away so that the knowledge outlives the people who carry it.
- Community group: https://www.facebook.com/groups/OWLOS - questions about
  the lessons, development stories, bug hunts, new builds.
- Source: https://github.com/KirinDenis/wire-city-2

GPL and is a tool that runs the programs, not part of their source. See
